lessons.title: Genetic Engineering: Applications and Implications
objectives: Explain how a gene is moved from one organism to another: cut out, joined in, carried into the host and read there
Describe the production of human insulin by bacteria, step by step
Give two more applications and state the benefits and the concerns of genetic engineering honestly
concepts: Restriction enzymes cut, ligase joins, a plasmid is the vector and the host cell makes the protein
Human insulin from E. coli is the worked application
GM crops and gene therapy are two more applications
The concerns are gene flow to wild species, cost and access, and editing human genes
lessons.content:
Genetic engineering, also called genetic modification, is the deliberate transfer of a gene from one organism to another so that the receiving organism makes a protein it could not make before. One named gene is cut out of the DNA of the donor organism, joined into the DNA of the recipient, and the recipient then reads that gene and makes the protein it codes for. An organism given a gene from another species is transgenic, and a crop or animal produced this way is a genetically modified organism (GMO). The difference from selective breeding is worth stating plainly: selective breeding crosses whole organisms over many generations and mixes thousands of genes at once, while genetic engineering moves one identified gene directly, and it can move a gene between species that could never interbreed, such as a human gene into a bacterium or a bacterial gene into a maize plant.

Four tools do the work. A restriction enzyme is the scissors: each one cuts DNA at a specific sequence of bases, and it cuts in a staggered way that leaves short single-stranded ends, called sticky ends, which pair with any other end cut by the same enzyme. Ligase is the glue: it joins the sugar-phosphate backbone of two DNA fragments that have been placed together, sealing the gene into its new DNA so that the two become one continuous molecule. A vector is the carrier that takes the gene into the cell, and the usual vector is a plasmid, a small ring of DNA found in a bacterium separate from its main chromosome; a plasmid is used because it is small, it is easy to cut open and close again, and the bacterium copies it every time it divides. A host cell is the cell that receives the gene and reads it, and the usual host is the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli), because it multiplies quickly, is easy to grow in large numbers in a fermenter and makes the protein cheaply. DNA made by joining a gene from one organism into the DNA of another is called recombinant DNA, and a marker gene, such as one giving resistance to an antibiotic, is often joined in at the same time so that the cells that took up the plasmid can be picked out from the many that did not.

Worked application: human insulin. People with diabetes cannot make enough insulin, the hormone that lowers blood glucose, and for many years the insulin they were given was extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Human insulin is now made by bacteria, in six steps. (1) Cut out the gene: the human insulin gene is identified in human DNA and cut out with a restriction enzyme. (2) Cut the vector: a plasmid is taken from a bacterium and cut open with the same restriction enzyme, so that its cut ends and the gene's cut ends are matching sticky ends. (3) Join them: the insulin gene is placed into the opened plasmid and ligase seals the joins, giving a recombinant plasmid, that is, a plasmid carrying a human gene. (4) Put it into the host: the recombinant plasmid is taken up by bacteria (E. coli), which now carry the human insulin gene. (5) Grow the host: those bacteria are grown in large numbers in a fermenter at a controlled temperature, pH and oxygen supply, with nutrients; every time a bacterium divides it copies the plasmid too, and because the bacteria read the human gene they make human insulin. (6) Extract and purify: the insulin is collected and purified, then tested and bottled for patients. The product is human insulin: the same sequence of amino acids as human insulin, made in a bacterium.

Two more applications, named but not worked here. Genetically modified crops: a gene is added to a crop plant to give it a useful characteristic, such as resistance to an insect pest (Bt maize and Bt cotton carry a bacterial gene for a protein that kills the larvae that eat the plant), resistance to a herbicide so that weeds can be killed without harming the crop, tolerance of drought or salt, or a higher yield or better nutritional content. Gene therapy: a normal copy of a gene is put into the cells of a patient who has a faulty copy, so that the cells can make the protein they could not make before; it has been used for conditions caused by a single faulty gene, such as some forms of severe combined immunodeficiency, and in trials for cystic fibrosis, and the gene is carried into the patient's cells by a vector, often a modified virus that has been altered so that it cannot cause disease.

The implications, honestly, on both sides. The benefits: insulin from bacteria does not depend on the supply of animal pancreases, so it can be made in large quantities, it is pure and consistent, and it carries no risk of passing on an animal disease, which matters to a person who needs insulin every day; GM crops can resist pests and so need fewer chemical sprays, which lowers the farmer's costs and reduces the harm those sprays do to non-target insects, and a crop can be given drought tolerance or a higher yield where food is short; gene therapy offers a way to treat a disease at its cause rather than only its symptoms.

The concerns, stated as concerns and not as proven harms. Genes crossing into wild species: pollen from a GM crop can be carried by wind or insects to a wild relative, and the added gene can then appear in wild plants, so a herbicide-resistance gene reaching a weed would make that weed harder to control; whether this happens, and how far, depends on the crop and on whether a wild relative grows nearby. Cost and access: GM seed is usually patented and must be bought again each season, so it costs more than saved seed and a small farmer may not be able to afford it, and the same is true of a new medicine, since a treatment that exists is no use to a patient who cannot pay for it. Ethical questions about editing human genes: changing a gene in a body cell affects only that patient, but changing a gene in an egg, a sperm or an early embryo changes every cell of the future person and is passed on to their children, who had no say in it, and editing to remove a disease is not the same thing as editing to choose a characteristic. Other concerns often raised, and worth naming: an allergic reaction to a new protein in a food, harm to non-target organisms, and the loss of traditional varieties as GM varieties spread. Each of these is a risk to be tested and monitored rather than a proven harm, which is why GM organisms are regulated and must be approved before they are grown or sold.

In an exam, expect either the procedure as a sequence (gene, then plasmid, then bacterium, then product) or a question asking for one benefit and one concern, each stated in its own terms.

lessons.title: Nervous System and Sense Organs
objectives: Describe the structure and function of the nervous system
Explain what happens in a reflex action
Describe how the eye responds to light and how hormones help to coordinate the body
concepts: The neuron is the basic unit of the nervous system
The cerebellum controls balance and the medulla controls heart rate and breathing
Reflex actions are rapid, automatic and protective
The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye; cones detect colour
Adrenaline produces the 'fight or flight' response
lessons.content:
The nervous system lets the body detect changes (stimuli) and respond to them quickly. It consists of the central nervous system, the brain and the spinal cord, together with the nerves that run to every part of the body. Its basic unit is the neuron, a cell specialised to carry electrical impulses. Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and motor neurons carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands.

A stimulus is any change in the environment that an organism can detect, and every response to one follows the same general path: stimulus, then receptor, then coordinator, then effector, then response. A receptor is a cell or a group of cells that detects the stimulus and starts an impulse; the coordinator is the part that decides what should be done about it, which in a vertebrate is the brain or the spinal cord; an effector is the part that carries out the response, and it is a muscle or a gland. The three receptors you are expected to name are the retina, which detects light, the taste buds, which detect chemicals dissolved in food, and the skin, which detects temperature and pain. The effectors are the muscles, which contract, and the glands, which secrete a hormone or another substance. So the stimulus of bright light is detected by the retina, coordinated by the brain and answered by the muscles of the iris, which change the size of the pupil.

Different parts of the brain have different jobs. The cerebrum is responsible for conscious thought, memory and voluntary movement; the cerebellum controls balance and coordination; and the medulla controls automatic processes such as heart rate and breathing. A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response that protects the body, such as pulling your hand away from a hot object. In a reflex, the impulse passes from the receptor along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord and straight back out along a motor neuron to the muscle, without waiting for the brain to decide, which is why the response is so fast.

The eye is a sense organ. Light enters through the cornea and the pupil; the iris, the coloured ring of muscle, changes the size of the pupil to control how much light enters, and the lens focuses the light onto the retina at the back of the eye. The retina contains two kinds of receptor: rods, which detect light intensity, and cones, which detect colour.

Seeing clearly at different distances is called accommodation, and the lens is the part that changes. The lens is held in place by the suspensory ligaments, which are joined to the ciliary muscles that form a ring around it. To see something distant the ciliary muscles relax, so the ring widens, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and they pull the lens thin, which is less curved; a thin lens bends the light less, and light from a distant object needs little bending, so the image still falls on the retina. To see something near the ciliary muscles contract, so the ring narrows, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens springs back thick, which is more curved; a thick lens bends the light more, which is what brings a near object's image back onto the retina. Say it the other way round as well, because examiners ask it in both directions: a thin lens, produced by relaxed ciliary muscles and taut suspensory ligaments, focuses a distant object on the retina, and a thick lens, produced by contracted ciliary muscles and slack suspensory ligaments, focuses a near object on the retina. In both cases the image is focused on the retina; what changes is how much the lens bends the light.

The pupil reflex is a reflex, and it uses the same arc as the withdrawal reflex above, a receptor, a sensory neurone, the coordinator, a motor neurone and an effector, with the iris as the effector instead of an arm muscle. In bright light the receptors in the retina detect the high light intensity and send impulses along the optic nerve to the brain; the brain sends impulses along a motor neurone to the iris, where the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil becomes smaller and less light enters. In dim light the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax, so the pupil widens and more light enters. It is a reflex because it is automatic and protective: it happens without a conscious decision, and it protects the retina from being damaged by too much light. You do not decide to do it, and you cannot stop it by deciding to.

Two defects of vision are corrected with lenses. In short sight (myopia) the eyeball is too long from front to back, or the lens is too strong, so the light is bent too much and the image focuses in front of the retina instead of on it; distant objects are blurred while near objects are seen clearly, and the correction is a concave, diverging lens, which spreads the light outwards a little before it reaches the eye so that the image moves back onto the retina. In long sight (hyperopia) the eyeball is too short or the lens is too weak, so the light is not bent enough and the image would focus behind the retina; near objects are blurred while distant objects are seen clearly, and the correction is a convex, converging lens, which bends the light inwards a little more so that the image moves forward onto the retina. A cataract is the lens becoming cloudy, which scatters the light and makes vision blurred and dim, and it is treated by replacing the lens.

Hormones also help to coordinate the body. Adrenaline, released by the adrenal glands, produces the 'fight or flight' response to danger by increasing the heart rate and breathing rate and releasing glucose into the blood.

lessons.title: Plant and Animal Movement and Support
objectives: Explain why support and movement are different problems for a plant and for an animal, and compare an exoskeleton, an internal bony skeleton and a hydrostatic skeleton
Name the five functions of the human skeleton and the two kinds of joint, and tell a ligament from a tendon
Work the antagonistic pair across the elbow in both directions, and describe how a plant is supported and how it moves
concepts: A plant stands on turgid cells and lignified xylem and cannot move its whole body; an animal is supported by a skeleton and moved by muscles
An exoskeleton, an internal bony skeleton and a hydrostatic skeleton each trade one advantage for one cost: moulting, enclosure, or no protection at all
The human skeleton supports, protects, gives muscle attachment, makes blood cells in the marrow and stores calcium
A hinge joint (elbow, knee) moves in one plane and a ball-and-socket joint (shoulder, hip) moves in all planes; ligaments join bone to bone and tendons join muscle to bone
A muscle can only pull, so the elbow needs an antagonistic pair: the biceps contracts to flex it and the triceps contracts to extend it
lessons.content:
Support and movement are two different problems, and a plant and an animal solve them differently. A plant is anchored by its roots and spends its whole life where the seed germinated, so its problem is support alone: it has to hold its leaves up to the light and its flowers up for pollination, and that is all. Its support comes from its own cells and from the walls of its water pipes, which the last part of this lesson describes. An animal has to move its whole body from place to place to find food, escape a predator and find a mate, so it needs two things a plant does not have: a skeleton to support the body and muscles to move it. A plant can bend towards the light, but it cannot walk.

An animal's skeleton is one of three kinds, and each is a trade-off rather than an improvement on the others. An exoskeleton is a hard case on the outside of the body, as in a crab or an insect: it protects the animal and gives the muscles a surface to pull against, but it cannot grow, so the animal has to moult, which means shedding it, and while the new case is still soft the animal is at its most vulnerable. An internal bony skeleton, an endoskeleton, is inside the body, as in a mammal: it is jointed, it grows with the animal and it gives large surfaces for muscle attachment, but it protects an organ only where bone encloses it. A hydrostatic skeleton is a body held firm by fluid under pressure inside a closed cavity, as in an earthworm: rings of circular and longitudinal muscles squeeze the fluid so that the worm shortens and extends, so it needs no hard parts at all and can squeeze through a narrow space, but the fluid gives no protection and cannot hold the animal up against gravity outside water.

The human skeleton is a bony endoskeleton and it does five jobs. It supports the body, holding it upright against gravity. It protects the delicate organs, with the skull enclosing the brain and the rib cage enclosing the heart and the lungs. It gives surfaces for muscles to attach to, so that a contracting muscle can pull a bone and move it. It produces blood cells, because the bone marrow inside bones such as the sternum, the ribs and the pelvis makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. And it stores minerals, mainly calcium and phosphate, which are released into the blood when other parts of the body need them. Learn all five, with the skull, the rib cage and the marrow as the examples that earn the marks.

A joint is a place where two bones meet, and two kinds are examined. A hinge joint allows movement in one plane only, like the hinge of a door: the elbow and the knee are hinge joints, and they bend and straighten in one direction and no other. A ball-and-socket joint allows movement in all planes, because a rounded end sits in a cup-shaped socket: the shoulder and the hip are ball-and-socket joints, and they swing forwards, backwards, sideways and round. Joints are held together and moved by two kinds of strap, and this is the pair students confuse. A ligament joins bone to bone: it holds the joint together and stops it moving too far, and the ligaments on either side of the knee joint are the ones that do it, though you can neither see nor feel them. A tendon joins muscle to bone: it carries the pull of the muscle to the bone, and it is the cord you can feel at the back of your ankle above the heel. If you cannot remember which one is which, ask what each one joins, because that is the only difference between them.

A muscle can only pull, never push: it shortens as it contracts, and when it relaxes it lengthens again, but it cannot force a bone back the other way. So any bone that has to move in two directions needs two muscles, one pulling each way, and two muscles that work against each other like this are called an antagonistic pair. The elbow is the worked example, and in an exam it is asked for as a labelled diagram, so here it is described in words. The upper arm has one bone, the humerus, running from the shoulder to the elbow, and the forearm has two, the radius and the ulna, running on from the elbow. The biceps lies in front of the humerus and the triceps behind it. The biceps runs from the shoulder blade, crosses the front of the humerus, and its tendon joins the radius just below the elbow; the triceps runs from the shoulder blade and the back of the humerus, and its tendon joins the ulna at the point of the elbow. To bend, or flex, the elbow the biceps contracts: it becomes shorter and fatter, and because its tendon is fixed to the radius it pulls the forearm up towards the shoulder, while the triceps relaxes, lengthens and is simply carried along. To straighten, or extend, the elbow the triceps contracts and pulls the forearm back down, while the biceps relaxes and lengthens. At every moment one of the pair is contracted and the other is relaxed, which is why the pair is described as antagonistic rather than cooperative. The same arrangement works the knee, where the quadriceps at the front of the thigh straightens the leg and the hamstrings at the back of it bend the leg.

How a plant is supported. A plant cell that is full of water is turgid: the water pushes outwards on the cell wall, the cell is firm, and a stem packed with firm cells is stiff enough to stand up. That is why a plant wilts when it loses water faster than the roots can replace it, because the cells lose their turgor and the stems and leaves droop. The second support is in the xylem, whose vessel walls are thickened with lignin, a hard waterproof material: the thickening stops the tubes collapsing and gives the stem real strength, and it is what holds a tall woody stem upright long after its older cells have stopped being turgid. Plant movement is slower and smaller than animal movement. A tropism is a growth movement in response to a stimulus coming from one direction: phototropism is a shoot growing towards the light and geotropism is a root growing downwards with gravity, and both are taught in Transport and Growth in Plants, so revise them there rather than here. The movement to add is the support movement of a climbing plant: a tendril is a modified leaf or stem that grows in a spiral, and when it touches a support it coils around it and holds the plant up, so that a weak-stemmed plant reaches the light without building a thick trunk.

lessons.title: Disease and Pathogens
objectives: State what a pathogen is and give examples of each kind
Distinguish communicable from non-communicable diseases
Describe how named diseases are caused and spread
concepts: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa
Communicable diseases pass from person to person, directly or through vectors
Non-communicable diseases are not spread between people
Malaria is caused by the Plasmodium protozoan, spread by the Anopheles mosquito
lessons.content:
A disease is a condition that stops the body working normally. A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease; the main groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa (protists). Diseases caused by pathogens are communicable (infectious), because they can be passed from one person to another, either directly or through a vector such as an insect.

Non-communicable diseases are not spread between people. Heart disease, diabetes, asthma and most cancers develop instead from a combination of lifestyle, diet, genes and environment, so they cannot be caught from someone who has them.

Examples you need to know. Influenza (flu) is caused by a virus, while cholera is caused by a bacterium and spreads in water or food contaminated by sewage — it produces severe watery diarrhoea that quickly leads to dehydration. Tuberculosis and typhoid are also bacterial. Malaria is caused by the Plasmodium protozoan, which is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, and dengue fever is caused by a virus transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which bites during the day and breeds in standing water near homes.

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is transmitted through blood, semen and other body fluids when they pass from one person to another. The safest way to prevent its spread is to avoid unprotected sex and never to share needles, and donated blood is screened before use. Because bacteria and viruses are different kinds of organism, antibiotics work only against bacteria and have no effect on viral diseases such as influenza, dengue or HIV.

A mosquito passes through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult. The egg, larva and pupa all live in standing water, and only the adult is on the wing. That is why the two vectors named above are controlled at the larval stage in the same way, but at the adult stage in different ways. Drain or cover anything that holds water, such as drums, tyres and flower pots, so that no egg can develop into a larva. Pour a film of oil on water that cannot be drained, so the larvae cannot reach the air and drown, and use a larvicide in water that has to be stored. The night-biting Anopheles is kept away with a bed net and window screens, and the day-biting Aedes aegypti with repellent and clothing that covers the skin. Clear rubbish so that no container is left to collect rain, because a single discarded container is enough to breed a new batch of adults.

Disease has social and economic effects that reach past the patient. Illness keeps a student out of school and an adult out of work, so lessons are missed and income stops. A family loses that income and at the same time spends on treatment, medicine and transport to a clinic, which can push it into debt. A country loses the productivity of its workers and spends a growing share of its health budget on treatment instead of prevention. An outbreak of a disease that visitors fear damages tourism, because cancelled bookings and travel warnings cost hotels, tour operators and the workers they employ. Stigma is an implication too: when a disease is treated as a disgrace, people avoid testing and treatment, so the disease spreads further among those who never came forward.

lessons.title: Body Defences and Immunity
objectives: Describe the body's first line of defence against pathogens
Explain the roles of phagocytes and lymphocytes
Explain how vaccination produces immunity
concepts: Skin, mucus, cilia and stomach acid stop pathogens entering the body
Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies
Vaccination makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease
lessons.content:
The body has several lines of defence against pathogens. The first line stops them getting in at all: the skin is a tough physical barrier, the airways are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs (cilia) that trap and sweep out microorganisms, and the hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills many microbes that are swallowed.

If a pathogen does get inside, white blood cells deal with it. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens, while lymphocytes produce antibodies. An antibody is a protein that locks onto the antigens on one particular pathogen and helps to destroy it, so each antibody is specific to one kind of pathogen. After an infection the body keeps some memory cells, so a second attack by the same pathogen is dealt with so quickly that no illness develops — this is natural immunity.

Vaccination gives immunity without the illness. A vaccine contains weakened, killed or harmless parts of a pathogen, and their antigens stimulate the lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells. If the real pathogen enters the body later, antibodies are made fast enough to stop the disease developing. Antibiotics are different from vaccines: they kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses.

A treatment acts on the pathogen after a person is infected: a medicine such as an antibiotic is given to cure the disease or hold it back in that patient. Control acts on the disease before it reaches other people: immunisation, vector control and a clean water supply reduce the number of people who ever become infected. The two work together, and control is what stops an outbreak.

Drug resistance comes from the misuse of antibiotics. Bacteria vary, and a course of antibiotics kills the susceptible ones first; the bacteria that survive are the ones that resist the drug, and they multiply. The antibiotic then works less well, or not at all, for the next patient. That is why a course must be finished even after the patient feels better, why antibiotics must not be taken for a virus such as a cold or influenza on which they have no effect, and why they must never be shared with another person.

Jamaica's public immunisation programme protects children against the main childhood diseases: BCG against tuberculosis, polio drops, and combined vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and measles. The programme works because of numbers: when a high proportion of a population is immunised, the pathogen has too few susceptible people left to pass to, and an outbreak cannot start.

lessons.title: Drug Abuse and Its Effects
objectives: State what a drug is and distinguish a medicine from drug abuse
Name the three classes of drug and give a real example of each
Describe the effect of named drugs on named organs and systems
Explain tolerance and withdrawal as the mechanism of addiction
Outline the social and economic effects of drug abuse, and the help available
concepts: A drug is a substance that alters the way the body or the mind works; alcohol and tobacco are drugs too, not only illegal substances

Depressants slow the nervous system (alcohol, heroin, inhaled solvents), stimulants speed it up (nicotine, cocaine, caffeine) and hallucinogens distort what the user sees and hears (LSD, cannabis at a high dose)
Tolerance is needing more of the drug for the same effect; withdrawal is the symptoms that appear when a dependent user stops
Addiction is a health condition that needs treatment, not a sign of weakness
Shared needles spread HIV and hepatitis B, and a pregnant user passes drugs to the fetus
lessons.content:
A drug is a substance that alters the way the body or the mind works. A medicine is a drug used to prevent, treat or cure a disease, taken in a measured dose. Drug abuse is the use of a drug in a way that harms the user's health or their ability to live and work: too much, too often, or for a purpose the drug is not meant for. A drug is not the same thing as an illegal drug. Alcohol and tobacco are drugs too, and although they are legal for adults, they are abused in exactly the same way and they cause dependence and organ damage just as illegal drugs do.

Drugs are grouped by what they do to the nervous system. Depressants slow it down: alcohol, heroin, and the solvents and glues that are inhaled. Stimulants speed it up: nicotine in tobacco, cocaine, and caffeine. Hallucinogens distort what the user sees, hears and feels: LSD, and cannabis when it is taken in a high dose. A different textbook may put a particular drug in a different class, but every class describes the drug's main action on the nervous system, so the examples above are the ones you can justify in an answer.

The drugs above each harm a named part of the body. Alcohol damages the liver, causing cirrhosis, and it slows judgement and reaction time, so the user misjudges speed, distance and risk. Tobacco damages the lungs: tar coats the airways and the alveoli and is a cause of bronchitis and lung cancer, and nicotine is the drug that makes the habit so hard to break. Cannabis impairs concentration and memory, which is a particular risk to a developing teenage brain. Cocaine raises the heart rate and blood pressure and can damage the heart, while heroin slows breathing and can kill by overdose, and heroin addiction is very hard to break. Solvents attack the brain and the heart, and a single session can cause sudden death. A pregnant user passes alcohol, nicotine and other drugs across the placenta to the fetus, so the unborn child is affected too.

Addiction is a change in the brain, not a moral failing. A drug releases dopamine in the brain's reward pathway, so the brain learns to want the drug and to repeat whatever produced it. Repeated use makes the brain respond less to the same amount, and this is tolerance: the user needs more of the drug for the same effect. When a dependent user stops, the body produces withdrawal: shaking, sweating, sickness and a craving that is hard to resist, and that craving is what drives the user back to the drug. Because tolerance and withdrawal are both physical, addiction is a health condition that needs treatment, not a sign of weakness.

The harm reaches past the user. Money is spent on the drug instead of food or school fees. An adult loses a job and a student drops out of school. Violence and crime follow the trade and the need to pay for it, and families break up under the strain. When needles are shared, HIV and hepatitis B pass from one user to the next, so drug abuse becomes a route for disease through a whole community.

The law treats drugs in two groups. In Jamaica alcohol and tobacco are legal for adults, but it is an offence to sell them to a child. Cannabis, cocaine and heroin are controlled drugs, so possessing them or supplying them to anyone is an offence. The law does not make a legal drug harmless: alcohol and tobacco still damage the body in the ways described above.

Prevention is cheaper than cure. Education that gives the facts, a supportive home, sport and clubs that fill the time a drug would take, and the decision to refuse the first offer all work better than trying to stop once addiction has started. Treatment is available through health services and counselling, and a user who wants to stop should be helped, not shamed.

lessons.title: Reproduction and Development
objectives: Distinguish asexual from sexual reproduction
Describe reproduction in flowering plants and in humans
Explain the function of the placenta
concepts: Asexual reproduction uses one parent and gives identical offspring (budding, binary fission)
Sexual reproduction uses two gametes and gives variation
The father's sperm (X or Y) determines the sex of a child
lessons.content:
Reproduction is the process by which organisms produce new individuals. In asexual reproduction only one parent is involved, so the offspring are genetically identical to it; examples are budding in yeast, binary fission in bacteria and amoeba, and the cuttings that gardeners take from plants. In sexual reproduction a male gamete and a female gamete fuse at fertilisation, so the offspring receive a mixture of genes from both parents and therefore vary.

In a flowering plant the male gamete is carried inside a pollen grain, which is produced by the anther. After pollination, the pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovule, and fertilisation happens when the male gamete from the pollen tube fuses with the egg cell in the ovule. The ovule develops into the seed and the ovary around it becomes the fruit.

In humans, sperm are produced in the testes and eggs are released from the ovaries. A sperm fuses with an egg in the oviduct (the fallopian tube) to form a zygote, which travels to the uterus and implants in its lining; the foetus then develops in the uterus for about nine months. The foetus is supported by the placenta, an organ that lets oxygen and nutrients diffuse from the mother's blood into the foetus's blood and lets carbon dioxide and other waste products diffuse back the other way, while keeping the two blood supplies separate. The sex of the child is determined by the father's sperm: every egg carries an X chromosome, so a sperm carrying an X makes a girl and a sperm carrying a Y makes a boy.

lessons.title: Living Things and Classification
objectives: List the characteristics shared by all living things
Explain why living things are classified
Use the classification groups and binomial naming system
concepts: Living things move, respire, respond to stimuli, grow, reproduce, excrete and feed
Classification groups run from Kingdom down to Species
A binomial name is the genus followed by the species (Homo sapiens)
lessons.content:
All living things share seven life processes. They move, respire to release energy from food, respond to stimuli (sensitivity), grow, reproduce, excrete the waste products of metabolism, and take in nutrition. A non-living object may show one or two of these features, but never all seven, so the whole list is what separates living from non-living things.

There are millions of different organisms, so biologists classify (group) them. Classification makes it easier to study living things and shows how they are related: the more groups two organisms share, the more closely related they are. The main groups, from the largest and most general to the smallest and most specific, are Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species, and every species is placed in all seven.

Each species has a two-part scientific (binomial) name, written in italics, in which the genus comes first with a capital letter and the species second with a small letter. Humans are Homo sapiens: Homo is the genus and sapiens is the species. Biologists all over the world use these names because a common name such as 'snapper' or 'papaw' can mean different organisms in different islands.
